Why understanding users and products isn’t enough when you don’t understand how decisions actually move through an organisation. For months, I was approaching product problems in a way that seemed entirely reasonable: research, analysis, process mapping, recommendations, documentation and workshops. I understood the product, I understood the users, and I could identify problems, gather evidence and propose solutions. And yet some well-supported recommendations still did not lead to decisions. The obvious reaction is to improve the recommendation: add evidence, explain it differently, prepare a better presentation, or document the reasoning more thoroughly. Sometimes that is exactly what is needed. But sometimes the problem is somewhere else. The person you work with every day is not necessarily the person who makes the decision. The person presenting your recommendation may not have the authority to approve it, while the person with the strongest influence may not even be present in the meetings where the work is discussed. At that point, the problem is no longer only about design. It is about understanding how decisions actually move through an organisation. There is another system to map As product designers, we map systems constantly: user journeys, processes, dependencies, information architecture, service interactions and product flows. We do this because understanding relationships helps us understand why something behaves the way it does. But organisations have another, less visible system made up of people, relationships, influence and decisions. I recently came across the User Experience University article Relationship Mapping for UX Leadership Success . It gave a useful framework for something I had already been encountering in practice: understanding stakeholders is not only about identifying who they are, but also about understanding relationships, influence, support and resistance around the work. That distinction matters. An organisational chart tells you who reports to whom, and a project structure tells you who is assigned to the work. Neither necessarily tells you how a product decision will actually get made . Your stakeholder is not necessarily your decision-maker A designer may work directly with a Product Owner, Product Manager or another stakeholder who understands the problem and supports the recommendation. But that person may still need approval from someone else. Another team may control the budget or implementation. A manager who has never attended the research sessions may have the final say, while several other people may influence the decision without formally owning it. This creates a gap between the environment in which a recommendation is created and the environment in which it is eventually judged. The recommendation may leave the room without the designer. And that changes how I think about product communication. Better documentation does not necessarily fix a broken communication path One response to this problem is to make recommendations increasingly self-contained. I have done this myself: preparing materials that preserve context, evidence and reasoning so that another person can carry the recommendation further into the organisation without losing its meaning. This is useful, but there is a limit to what better documentation can solve. A document cannot tell you whether it reached the person who matters. It cannot guarantee that the strongest evidence survived a verbal summary or show whether someone with significant influence opposed the proposal before it reached the decision-maker. So another question becomes necessary: What happens to the recommendation after it leaves the room? That question moves us beyond stakeholder management and towards understanding the decision path itself. Influence is part of product work Designers are trained to focus on the quality of the solution, while senior designers increasingly learn to focus on outcomes. But there is a connection between those two things that is easy to underestimate. A solution that cannot enter the decision-making process has very little chance of becoming a product outcome. This does not mean designers should become organisational politicians. It means that understanding the environment in which decisions happen is part of understanding the constraints of the product. If a recommendation needs to travel through three people before reaching the person who can approve it, that path matters. If one stakeholder owns the problem but another owns the budget, that matters. If the person with the most knowledge has the least decision authority, that matters. These are not interpersonal details surrounding product work; they affect whether product work can produce change.
